lesson.title: Principal Branches: Taming the Trig Functions
lesson.summary: Because sine, cosine, and tangent repeat forever, none of them is one to one on its natural domain, so every inverse trig function is secretly built by first restricting to a single principal branch, and that choice shapes every derivative formula in this unit.
lesson.body:
The equation sin x = 1/2 has infinitely many solutions: pi/6, 5pi/6, pi/6 plus any multiple of 2pi, and more. A function needs to be one to one, passing the horizontal line test, before it can have a genuine inverse. So before arcsin can even be defined, sine's domain has to be cut down to a single interval where it never repeats a value. The standard choice is [-pi/2, pi/2], where sine climbs steadily from -1 to 1, hitting every value in between exactly once. That restricted piece is called the principal branch, and arcsin is defined as its inverse.

The same idea applies to every trig function, each with its own restricted domain and resulting range. Sine restricted to [-pi/2, pi/2] gives arcsin with domain [-1,1] and range [-pi/2, pi/2]. Cosine restricted to [0, pi] gives arccos with domain [-1,1] and range [0, pi]. Tangent restricted to (-pi/2, pi/2) gives arctan with domain all reals and range (-pi/2, pi/2). Cotangent restricted to (0, pi) gives arccot with domain all reals and range (0, pi). Secant restricted to [0, pi/2) union (pi/2, pi] gives arcsec with domain |x| >= 1 and range that same two piece set. Cosecant restricted to [-pi/2, 0) union (0, pi/2] gives arccsc with domain |x| >= 1 and range that same two piece set.

The two piece ranges for arcsec and arccsc look unusual compared to the single intervals used for the other four, but the reason is simple: secant is undefined exactly at y = pi/2, and cosecant is undefined exactly at y = 0, so neither function can be restricted to one clean, uninterrupted interval that also stays one to one. The principal branch has to be built from two half open pieces glued around that forbidden midpoint. This is exactly why the derivatives of arcsec and arccsc, worked out in the two previous chapters, carry an absolute value: which of the two pieces an angle sits in depends on the sign of x, and |x| is what lets a single formula describe both pieces at once.

The restriction also explains a common point of confusion when evaluating these functions. The equation sin x = 1/2 has many solutions, but arcsin(1/2) has exactly one correct value: pi/6, because pi/6 is the only angle inside the principal branch [-pi/2, pi/2] whose sine is 1/2. The angle 5pi/6 also satisfies sin x = 1/2, but it lies outside the principal branch, so it is never a valid output of arcsin. This is also why the identity arcsin(sin x) = x is only guaranteed to hold when x already lies inside [-pi/2, pi/2]; outside that interval it can fail, a subtlety worth remembering whenever inverse trig functions are composed with their originals.
